query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Small additions of Al (up to ~5 at.%) in a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating promote the formation of a more protective oxide scale at elevated temperatures, which reduces abrasive and oxidative wear and suppresses local plastic deformation under sliding loads.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a metal substrate, with zero Al content.
generation.intervention: Incrementally increase Al content up to about 5 at.% in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
generation.conditions: Perform pin-on-disk measurements at 500–800 °C in air at comparable normal loads and sliding speeds for all samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Stable, adherent oxide scale enriched in Al and Cr forming on the coating surface at high temperature.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature sliding, the Al-enriched surface oxide layer reduces abrasive interactions and prevents microcracking in the near-surface region, leading to lower wear rates and reduced microscopic deformation compared to the baseline with no Al doping.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the no-Al baseline, coatings doped up to ~5 at.% Al will exhibit measurably decreased wear rates (potentially by at least a factor of two) and reduced subsurface plastic deformation in the 500–800 °C regime.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coating with 0 at.% Al under identical wear test parameters, resulting in higher wear rates and more apparent near-surface deformation at 500–800 °C.
generation.boundary: The protective benefit may be diminished below ~500 °C (where oxidation is less pronounced) or above ~800 °C (where oxide layers may degrade), and could also vary with load or contact geometry beyond pin-on-disk conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of wear reduction from Al doping could differ under more aggressive conditions or different alloy compositions, so results may not extrapolate beyond the specified temperature and doping ranges.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a pin-on-disk test comparing FeNiCrCoCu coatings with 0, 2, and 5 at.% Al doping at 500–800 °C in air using identical loads and sliding conditions.
measurements: Cross-sectional microstructure and oxide scale characterization (SEM, EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no detectable decrease in wear rate or suppression of local plastic deformation with increasing Al content, and no difference in oxide layer formation between Al-doped and undoped coatings, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4. Morphlology and Wear Mechanism of Wear Scars
cited_evidence.text: From the EDS, it can be seen that the O content on the surface is higher than that in the other samples, which indicates that this sample has experienced more severe oxidative wear during the frictional wear process. Combined with the above analysis, it can be seen that the alloy has a wear mechanism of abrasive wear, adhesive wear and oxidation wear in the process of friction and wear.

The fine-grained sample has higher surface hardness and mechanical strength, which is helpful to improve the wear resistance []. Compared with other materials, this can give us some inspiration for later work. The average wear rate of TiO2 10 wt.% NiAl coating deposited on the low alloy steel 40Cr4 surface is 9.821 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1, and the wear rate of TiO213 wt.% NiAl coating 40Cr4 is 1.22 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1 under the normal load of 10 N and sliding speed of 500 mm/s [], which is close to that of FG HEA under the load of 30 N and sliding speed of 5 mm/s. The wear rate of AlCrSiN-coated tool steel K340 is 5.681 × 10−7 mm3 N−1 m−1 under the load of 10 N and 10 cm/s []. The average wear rate of AlTiSiN + TiSiN coatings deposited on the H 13 tool steels is 2.30 × 10−8 and 1.31 × 10−8 mm3 N−1 m−1 for normal load of 30 and 50 N at the lubricated conditions, respectively []. Tubrication can effectively improve the wear resistance of materials, which presents good inspiration for our later work.

chosen.lever: aluminum doping level in the FeNiCrCoCu coating
chosen.technique: high-temperature pin-on-disk tribological testing combined with SEM/XRD analysis
chosen.conditions: baseline (no Al) vs. incremental Al content (up to 5 at.%), tested under sliding at 500–800 °C in air
chosen.why: Adding small amounts of Al to the FeNiCrCoCu matrix is a direct and standard route to modulate high-temperature oxide formation, which we hypothesize to govern wear resistance and local deformation under sliding. Prior work on high-entropy alloys suggests that Al additions can stabilize protective oxide scales, thereby potentially reducing wear and plastic flow at hot conditions. If Al doping does not lead to the expected reduction in wear or change in local deformation at elevated temperatures, this result would falsify the proposed mechanism.
